title: UnitedHealth vs. Clover Health: Which Stock Offers Better Growth? - TradingView
content: The U.S. health insurance industry is undergoing a strategic shift as rising medical utilization, evolving reimbursement policies and mounting healthcare costs reshape the operating landscape. The Medicare Advantage market, in particular, presents a mix of growth opportunities and profitability challenges, prompting insurers to prioritize disciplined pricing, technology integration and efficient care delivery. Against this backdrop, UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH and Clover Health Investments, Corp. CLOV offer exposure to two distinct business models within the evolving managed care space. UnitedHealth benefits from a diversified business structure spanning health insurance, healthcare services, pharmacy benefit management and data analytics. Clover Health, meanwhile, takes a more focused approach through its Medicare Advantage offerings and physician-centric technology platform designed to improve clinical decision-making and manage healthcare costs. While UnitedHealth’s strategy centers on scale and business integration, Clover Health emphasizes technology-enabled care delivery and operating efficiency. Their contrasting approaches warrant a closer examination of financial strength, profitability and sustainable growth prospects. Let’s dive deep and closely compare the fundamentals of the two stocks to determine which one is a better investment now. UnitedHealth's growth prospects are supported by the breadth of its UnitedHealthcare and Optum businesses. Its insurance operations are working to improve Medicare Advantage offerings through more disciplined pricing, benefit design and market selection. At the same time, Medicaid performance is expected to improve as pricing adjustments and medical cost management address the gap between reimbursement and healthcare costs. Its medical care ratio improved to 88.4% in the third quarter of 2026 from 89.9% a year ago. Continued pricing adjustments and operational improvements could support earnings recovery heading into 2027. UnitedHealth’s integrated business model remains a key competitive strength. Through Optum, the company combines healthcare delivery, pharmacy services and technology capabilities with its insurance operations. Its emphasis on integrated value-based care, preventive healthcare and complex disease management is aimed at improving patient outcomes while containing medical expenses. This approach could strengthen profitability and create opportunities for sustainable organic growth across its businesses. Technology is becoming increasingly central to UNH’s operational transformation. The company has expanded AI-enabled clinical chart summarization to more than 40% of its employed clinicians, reducing chart review time by 33%. It is also deploying AI-powered Medicare Advantage plan recommendations, simplifying prior authorization processes and automating administrative functions. These initiatives could improve productivity, enhance customer experience and lower operating expenses over time. Optum Rx remains another key growth driver as demand for specialty pharmacy services increases. The business is expanding its behavioral health pharmacy network, enhancing infusion services and adopting more transparent drug pricing models. More than half of Optum Rx’s membership now comes from outside UnitedHealthcare, reflecting its ability to attract external customers. Growing biosimilar adoption and closer integration of pharmacy and medical care could further strengthen the business’s earnings potential. Despite its recovery initiatives, UnitedHealth remains exposed to regulatory uncertainty, rising healthcare costs and reimbursement pressures. Changes to Medicare Advantage payment policies, star ratings and risk adjustment methodologies could weigh on profitability. Ongoing regulatory investigations and legal challenges add further uncertainty. Moreover, execution risks associated with restructuring its operations and improving Optum’s performance could slow its earnings recovery. Unlike UnitedHealth, which benefits from a broad healthcare ecosystem, Clover Health is building its growth strategy around a more focused proposition: using artificial intelligence to make Medicare Advantage more efficient and improve patient outcomes. Its proprietary Clover Assistant platform gives physicians data-driven insights to identify chronic conditions earlier, manage care more effectively and reduce healthcare costs. This technology-led approach is helping Clover expand its Medicare Advantage business while creating opportunities to improve profitability as its membership base matures. Medicare Advantage membership increased 45% year over year in the third quarter of 2026. Clover’s improving quality ratings add another dimension to its growth prospects. Its flagship PPO plan, which accounts for approximately 98% of its membership, secured a five-star rating for Payment Year 2028. Higher quality ratings could strengthen reimbursement economics and provide greater flexibility in designing competitive insurance products. Meanwhile, expanding membership and spreading fixed administrative expenses across a larger customer base could help CLOV achieve greater operating leverage. Beyond insurance, Clover is pursuing growth through Counterpart Health, which extends its clinical technology to external healthcare organizations. The initiative creates opportunities to serve third-party insurers, physician groups and accountable care organizations without relying exclusively on insurance membership expansion. Moreover, Clover expects 2026 to mark its first full year of GAAP profitability, projecting net income of $25-$35 million. Improving financial performance and a debt-free balance sheet could provide greater flexibility to finance technology investments and business expansion. However, Clover Health’s limited geographic diversification makes it more vulnerable to regional competition and changes in local market conditions than UnitedHealth. Its smaller operating scale could also limit its bargaining power with healthcare providers. Additionally, unexpected increases in medical utilization, changes in federal reimbursement policies and higher customer acquisition costs could pressure margins. Nevertheless, disciplined market expansion and effective expense management could help CLOV contain these risks. For UnitedHealth, the Zacks Consensus Estimate forecasts 2026 earnings per share (EPS) of $20.61, reflecting 26.1% year-over-year growth, followed by another 13.4% jump in 2027. For 2026, revenues are pegged at $449.1 billion, suggesting year-over-year growth of 0.4%. It has witnessed one positive earnings estimate revision over the past 30 days against no downward revisions. On the other hand, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Clover Health’s 2026 revenues indicates 55.6% year-over-year growth. The consensus estimate for 2026 earnings is pinned at 6 cents per share, signaling a 50% increase, followed by further growth of 183.2% in 2027.It has witnessed one positive earnings estimate revision over the past 30 days, with no downward revisions. Clover Health trades at a higher forward P/E of 23.31X versus UnitedHealth’s 14.80X, reflecting stronger growth expectations. Its technology-driven healthcare model, expanding Medicare Advantage membership and improving profitability prospects could justify the premium.Both are currently trading below their three-year median P/E multiples. Over the past year, UnitedHealth’s shares have gained 3.7%, underperforming Clover Health and the S&P 500’s growth of 51.4% and 5.3%, respectively. UNH currently trades below its average analyst price target of $478.28, implying a 42.3% potential upside from current levels. CLOV also trades below its average analyst price target of $5.60, implying a 48.2% potential upside from current levels. Both UnitedHealth and Clover Health offer exposure to the growing healthcare market, but CLOV currently has stronger growth momentum. While UNH benefits from its diversified operations, medical cost pressures and regulatory challenges could weigh on its recovery. CLOV's faster revenue growth, expanding Medicare Advantage membership, improving profitability and technology-driven care model make it an attractive growth opportunity. As such, CLOV appears to have a better hand at the moment, even though both companies currently carry a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). title: UMaine football ends season in a 24-21 loss to UNH - The Maine Campus
content: ORONO, Maine — On Saturday, Nov. 21, the University of Maine football team ended its season against the University of New Hampshire with a 24-21 loss. Maine came out strong with the first touchdown 10 minutes into the game from first-year wide receiver Ty Boone. Redshirt second-year kicker Samuel Tremblay completed the extra point to give the Black Bears seven points. They could not hold on to the lead for long, as UNH came back with a touchdown with four minutes left in the first quarter from graduate student running back Myles Thomason to tie it up. Maine was able to take back the lead with a deep pass from redshirt first-year quarterback Michale McMaugh to redshirt second-year running back Rashawn Marshall for a touchdown. Maine closed out the second quarter tied at 21-21 to enter halftime. In the third quarter, the score stayed the same with not much action. Going into the last quarter, the Wildcats got a field goal from second-year kicker Lucas Glassburn that secured the three winning points for UNH to win the game 24-21. This loss concluded Maine’s 2026 season with a disappointing 1-10 overall record. Maine lost 10 straight games, a program-record losing streak. The team’s only win came in the first game of the season, a 21-18 victory against Towson University, which created belief and hope for the rest of the season. Unfortunately, this was not the case, as Maine went on to lose 55-3 against Appalachian State University the next week and every game since. A unique moment in the season was the rotation of three different quarterbacks. In some games, the coaching staff would switch quarterbacks for every offensive play, which is almost never done in football. At the beginning of the season, redshirt second-year Eddie Buehler was the starting quarterback for the Black Bears after competing against redshirt third-year Caden Drezek in the preseason. Halfway through the regular season, when nothing was working offensively, the staff decided to mix things up and alternate between Buehler and Drezek for offensive plays. Drezek performed well under pressure and earned the starting quarterback position until the last two games, when McMaugh played full games as a third-string quarterback. Anybody can tell that Maine had offensive difficulties this entire season just by looking at the scores. The team tried to fix this problem by firing offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters on Oct. 5, in the middle of the season, which is uncommon. Waters was replaced by running backs coach Sean Green. “Those are decisions that are really hard and affect everyone,” said head coach Jordan Stevens. “There’s a lot that goes into that to do what’s best for the football team and put us in a better position to win.” The Black Bears will have time to assess the season during the break and look to rebuild during the spring to hopefully come back with a better record next season.
